Issued at 139 PM CDT Mon Aug 10 2026

West to northwest flow continues aloft over the region per a weak 
broad ridge over the western CONUS. Another weak embedded shortwave 
(500mb winds 35-45kts) will track east/southeast across SD this 
evening into IA/MN through early Tuesday morning with the bulk of 
the vorticity over central through southeastern SD. At the surface, 
a weak low will be over southwestern SD this evening with an 
inverted trough extending northeastward from it through SD/MN 
through the overnight hours with not much movement with the low and 
a slight track southeast with the trough. 700mb temps are not overly 
strong, ranging from +8 to +14C this evening, warmest over south 
central SD. With 850mb to sfc winds out of the south and southeast, 
this continues to usher in warm moist air with dewpoints rising into 
the upper 60s to potentially lower 70s, before winds switch more 
east/northeast overnight. There is no lack of instability with HREF 
mean CAPE between 2000-3500j/kg (RAP=3000-4000j/kg) this evening to 
around 1500-2500j/kg by 06Z with the highest amounts over 
central through southeastern SD. Bulk shear will range between 
40-50kts through the overnight with 0-3km SRH 200-400m2s2, 
highest over south central through east central SD, and steep 
low to mid level lapse rates. Only thing really lacking is a 
strengthening LLJ overnight.

This sets the stage for showers and thunderstorms to fire up 
starting this evening as the cap erodes, however, it remains tricky 
with several potential outcomes. Overall consensus per CAMS has 
discrete cells/clusters developing over north central SD/ND and 
potentially one over south central/southern SD. This earlier stage 
of development and storms tracking over central SD is when the 
largest hail (potentially over 2") and the threat of tornadoes
would be with any supercells given surface based storms 
interacting with surface trough (and moderate Cape/shear) with 
0-1km SRH between 100-200m2s2 and stp of 1. As mergers and 
additional development occurs, storms will grow quickly upscale 
as they track east/southeast into an organized cluster (MCS) 
with possible bowing segments if an RIJ develops. However, 
HRRR/REFS has nothing developing until around midnight with 
storm mode being more clustery over east central through 
southeastern SD. Between the individual CAMS, there are 
differences in where these storms initially develop, whether 1 
or 2 areas of convection will merge or track separately, 
timing/location of upscale growth to a MCS, if bowing segments 
do form, and and exact track of it. Due to this, confidence is 
very low on which scenario will play out at this time. So 
continued with sticking with the NBM for pops given this 
uncertainty which does a good job, keeping pops broad due with 
highest pops (50-75%) over central through east central SD where
the majority of the CAMS show this area being impacted the 
greatest and where our best instability lies and energy aloft. 
Another caveat is the ongoing thick smoke from the PacNW 
blanketing the region. If thick enough, this could damper 
instability and convection and we get little in the way of 
storms.

With this, there is a Slight Risk (level 2/5) per SPC for much of 
the CWA (with the exception of far NESD/MN which is in a marginal 
risk) for the potential of scattered severe storms. There is a cig 1 
hail threat (potential 2"+ in diameter) given supercell potential, 
mainly along and west of a line from Aberdeen to Huron. SPC has 
added in a 2% tornado threat along and south of a line from Mobridge 
to Redfield where tornadoes are possible mentioned above. Wind gusts 
of 60-70 mph are possible with the potential for winds in excess of 
75mph if an MCS develops especially for locations where the 
potential bowing system could track. Therefore a Cig 1 is 
outlooked for wind mainly along and east and southeast of a line
from Gettysburg to Pierre where some of the CAMs indicate this 
greatest potential. 

Not much change aloft Tuesday and Wednesday in ongoing west to 
northwest flow aloft and potentially weak embedded shortwaves tracking 
across the region and a front tracking southward out of Canada 
Wednesday evening/night. Adding in daytime heating/instability and 
ongoing low level moisture and shear, we will continue with the
threat of showers and thunderstorms each afternoon/evening into
the overnight hours. A Sight Risk (level 2/5) is in place 
mainly west of the James River and a Marginal Risk ( level 1/5) 
east of James River Tuesday. A Marginal Risk extends along and
south of a line from Eagle Butte to Brookings Wednesday. Broad 
ridge that has been over the western CONUS will shift eastward 
and over the central CONUS for the end of the week. Add in 
surface features and additional instability and chances for 
showers and thunderstorms continue through the end of the week 
with low confidence this far out on any severe weather 
potential. As of now ML guidance kee
